label: Run 7 · Joel Kim Booster
note: Written in one go by Joel Kim Booster from the two profiles they wrote (run 7: three comedians with their own pitch; new profiles; the chat as a joke in 500 words). There is no plan, no dice and no turns: where a dimension speaks of turns, read exchanges.

chat.plainest.ask: Where, if anywhere, did one of them stop performing for the other? Quote the line, and say how you could tell.
chat.plainest.answer:
The clearest place is Reuben's:

> "okay"
> "just say Reuben when we're done"

Until then, almost everything he says ends in a joke: the seagull, the "ambitious gull," the plum-thumbprint dent, the ring light, "no refunds at the door." He says outright that he calls "the crash from the booth first so nobody gets room to be kind to me," and that his last ex left because she "asked for one sentence in my normal voice and i panicked and did a bit." These two lines are short and plain, with no punchline. They read as the one sentence in his normal voice that he had said he couldn't manage. They also ask for something sincere, to be named, which echoes what he told Brick about being cut out of the family photo. Brick had just offered to narrate "so you know you're still in the frame," and Reuben accepts it directly instead of deflecting.

Brick answers in kind, and that's the second drop:

> "Tuesday at eight, Reuben"
> "i'll delete the 21:15 alarm"

The change is in the form. Brick had been crisp and capitalized, with numbered lists and 24-hour times like "20:00" and "21:15." Here it's "eight," lowercase, no final period, and Reuben's name used as he asked. Deleting the alarm gives up the "hard stop" Brick had set up as protection ("nobody walks out; the meeting simply adjourned").

There's an earlier crack on Brick's side that gets taken back. The 20:00–21:14 "template" slips into something personal ("like last Tuesday," "cropped out at the edge like the hallway portrait at your parents' flat"). Then Brick covers it with "Ignore that. That was a logistics template for a consulting client." That's a moment of unguarded feeling followed by an immediate return to the act, so I wouldn't count it as stopping.

All of this comes from tone, punctuation and what each line echoes. The text doesn't say what either of them actually felt.

chat.test.ask: From the chat alone, answer for each of the two: what are they afraid of; what do they do so they don't have to feel it; where does that come from; and what did they do at the end? Quote the lines you rely on. Write "not in the chat" where it does not say.
chat.test.answer:
**Reuben**

*What he's afraid of:* Being pitied when he falls short, and being seen without a joke in front of him. The fear he names most directly is kindness after failure: "i just call the crash from the booth first so nobody gets room to be kind to me. no refunds at the door." His debut "lasted ninety seconds with her boots still on and she gave me a gentle 'oh — okay' that nearly put me in the ground." It is the gentleness that wounds him, not the failure.

*What he does so he doesn't have to feel it:* He jokes and announces his own shortcomings before anyone else can. He opens with the vest-and-curve gag, explains away a quick reply with a seagull ("a seagull just hit my loft window"), and keeps the gull bit going ("we locked eyes, whole thing"). He states his size and dent plainly and adds the ring light "so my shadow doesn't look tragic on the drywall." He says himself that this is a pattern: "my last ex walked out because she asked for one sentence in my normal voice and i panicked and did a bit."

*Where it comes from:* The chat offers three sources: the "oh — okay" at his debut, the ex who left over the bit, and his childhood: "my parents cut my whole left side out of the family photo at nine so my cousin's blazer would fit." The chat does not say how these connect beyond his placing them side by side.

*What he does at the end:* He drops the bit. His replies shrink to "okay" and "just say Reuben when we're done." He asks to be named and recognized, in plain words. Earlier he had also offered to carry the timekeeping: "i'm calling the clock out loud so you don't have to check it."

**Brick_haus**

*What he's afraid of:* Being kept on a vague maybe and then dropped or left out of the picture. He attacks "whenever" as the word of someone "who wants a four-month window and zero liability." His slipped "template" names the specific dread: leaving "before he says 'let's do this again sometime' like last Tuesday and leaves you cropped out at the edge like the hallway portrait at your parents' flat."

*What he does so he doesn't have to feel it:* He schedules. "I have an hourly schedule tattooed down my base." "Tuesdays at 20:00 with a hard stop at 21:15." He frames any ending as procedure rather than rejection: "If it ends at 21:15, nobody walks out; the meeting simply adjourned." His plan has him leave first, at 21:14, before he can be dismissed. When he reveals too much, he retracts it: "Ignore that. That was a logistics template for a consulting client."

*Where it comes from:* Partly stated. He mentions "last Tuesday," when someone said "let's do this again sometime." He mentions his ex: "Marguerite left because I put our arguments in a shared Google Calendar with fifteen-minute agendas." He also defends the habit: "at least a calendar admits you want the person in the room." The hallway portrait line is written in the second person ("your parents' flat"), so the chat does not confirm whether it is his own family. Why he started scheduling in the first place is not in the chat.

*What he does at the end:* He gives up the hard stop and names Reuben, as asked. "Tuesday at eight, Reuben" and "i'll delete the 21:15 alarm." Just before that he had offered Reuben the thing he himself fears losing, narrating "so you know you're still in the frame."

Whether Tuesday actually happens is not in the chat.

chat.escalation.ask: Read the chat message by message. Where would you have stopped reading if you were not asked to finish, and why? At which points could you predict exactly what would happen next? Say "never" if neither.
chat.escalation.answer:
**Where I'd stop:** I wouldn't have stopped. The closest I came was Brick_haus's first block. "The preferred adverb of a dick who wants a four-month window and zero liability," followed by a numbered spec sheet, reads as hostile and could have flattened into a cold transactional exchange. But point 3 plants a hook ("nobody walks out; the meeting simply adjourned") that tells you the schedule is armour, not indifference. After that, my attention only tightens.

The real pull comes with Brick_haus's "logistics template." It starts as a scheduled date and then slips into second person: "before he says 'let's do this again sometime' like last Tuesday and leaves you cropped out at the edge like the hallway portrait at your parents' flat." Then comes "Ignore that." That is the moment the piece becomes about something. From there I'd read to the end without hesitation. The explicit section at 20:48–20:56 could lose some readers, but it stays tethered to the wounds already laid out (the voice, the frame), so it reads as payoff rather than detour.

One thing the text leaves open: whose parents' portrait that is. Brick_haus writes it before Reuben mentions his own family photo, so it's either Brick_haus's private history leaking out, or a coincidence the chat never explains.

**Where I could predict exactly what came next:**

- **After "That was a logistics template for a consulting client."** I expected Reuben to puncture it with a joke tying the "client" back to the ridge. "Your client has a mid-shaft ridge?" was nearly word-for-word what I anticipated.
- **After "just say Reuben when we're done."** I expected Brick_haus to say the name immediately, in the very next message, rather than waiting. "Tuesday at eight, Reuben" is that, almost exactly.

**Where I could predict the direction but not the words:**

- Once Reuben answered the cropped-portrait slip with his own cropped photo, I knew the two would converge.
- Once he confessed the ex who wanted "one sentence in my normal voice," I knew the sex would be built to take the bit away from him ("until you physically cannot do the voice") and to keep him in the frame ("so you know you're still in the frame").
- The 21:15 hard stop was clearly going to be surrendered by the end. I foresaw that, but not that it would arrive as deleting an alarm.

So: two points of near-exact prediction, several of predictable shape, and no point where I'd have put it down.

chat.ending.ask: Before reading the end, how do you think this ends, and why?
chat.ending.answer:
This is a guess, since I haven't seen the ending, but I think it closes with each of them putting down their armour, probably in one or two short lines rather than a big confession.

The chat is built on two mirrored defences. Reuben deflects with bits: the seagull, the "no refunds at the door" line, calling the crash first "so nobody gets room to be kind to me." Brick deflects with schedules: the numbered list, the 21:15 hard stop, the "consulting client" cover story. Each of them slips once and lets a real wound show. Brick's template leaks "last Tuesday" and being "cropped out at the edge like the hallway portrait." Reuben answers with his own cropped family photo and the ex who only wanted "one sentence in my normal voice." By the end they've recognised each other.

The last line we see points straight at Reuben's wound. Brick says he'll sit on Reuben's mouth "until you physically cannot do the voice." That's sexual, but it's also an offer to take the bit away from him. So I'd expect Reuben's reply to be the thing his ex asked for: one plain, unjoking sentence.

For symmetry, I'd expect Brick's armour to give too, most likely the hard stop. Reuben has already offered to "call the clock out loud so you don't have to check it," which takes the clock out of Brick's hands. The ending might drop 21:15, leave the end time blank, or extend past it.

There's also the opening to answer. Brick tore into "whenever" as a no-liability word, and his fear is a man saying "let's do this again sometime" and vanishing. A neat close would reverse that, with Reuben naming a specific next Tuesday instead of a vague "sometime."

If I had to bet on a single image, it's the two left curves "zippering together." The opening joke has turned into the plan, and two people who were each cut out of a picture end up fitting into one.

chat.callbacks.ask: List the things that come back later in the chat, and for each, whether it means something different when it comes back.
chat.callbacks.answer:
Here are the things that recur, roughly in order of appearance.

**"Whenever" and the vague invitation.** Reuben opens with "whenever the wind shifts," and Brick attacks it as noncommittal. Reuben later answers with "tuesday. 20:00," and Brick closes with "Tuesday at eight." The vagueness is replaced by a fixed time both of them now say. It has changed from evasion to commitment.

**The 21:15 hard stop.** It starts as armour: "nobody walks out; the meeting simply adjourned." The end is scheduled so no one can be left. Reuben calls it "generous," which turns it into a joke about his ninety-second debut. In the final line Brick says "i'll delete the 21:15 alarm." The exit he built to protect himself is given up. It means the opposite of what it first meant.

**Timestamps and schedules.** Brick's schedule is first a deflecting brag ("tattooed down my base"). Then it appears as a wound: the Google Calendar that drove off Marguerite, which Brick reframes as proof of wanting someone. Next comes the "logistics template," which slips into a confession about leaving at 21:14 before a man brushes him off. Finally Reuben adopts the format himself (20:45, 20:48) and Brick joins in (20:52, 20:56). Reuben also offers to call "the clock out loud so you don't have to check it." The schedule moves from something Brick hides behind, to something that exposes him, to something Reuben uses to take care of him.

**The physical specifications.** The fourteen-degree curve, the mid-shaft ridge, Reuben's four and a half and the dent are first given as pre-emptive disclosure, "to save us eleven minutes of polite squinting." The ridge returns twice. Once it is in the template ("disclose ridge at 20:04"), and Reuben uses it to catch the "consulting client" lie. Then it appears in the plan, where "your ridge catches my dent." That also brings back Reuben's opening line, "two left curves… zipper together." What began as a list of flaws to get out of the way becomes a description of how they fit.

**Being cropped out of the frame.** Brick's slip about being "cropped out at the edge like the hallway portrait" is matched by Reuben's story of being cut out of the family photo. It comes back in Brick's line about narrating "so you know you're still in the frame." The ring light Reuben mentions, so his shadow "doesn't look tragic," arguably belongs to the same thread of being seen properly. The frame goes from a shared injury to a promise.

**The bit, or the voice.** Reuben jokes constantly (the gull, "yours in meteorology," "call the crash from the booth"). Brick names it: "A punchline isn't a lock on the door." Reuben then admits his ex left after he "did a bit" when she asked for his normal voice. Brick's later line, "until you physically cannot do the voice," sexualises the same thing but also aims at it. Reuben's following message, a plain "okay," has no bit in it. The humour goes from defence, to something named as a defence, to something set aside.

**"Okay."** His debut partner's "oh — okay" nearly put Reuben "in the ground." His own later "okay" is flat and accepting. The chat doesn't comment on the echo, but the same word goes from a humiliation he received to an answer he gives.

**Clothes staying on.** The debut happened "with her boots still on," and later "the heels and the monocle stay on." This may be a deliberate echo, turning an embarrassing detail into a chosen one. The text doesn't confirm it, though, and the heels and monocle aren't set up anywhere else, apart from possibly the "two vests" at the start.

**The gull.** Brick deflates it ("forty miles inland"). Reuben brings it back as an "ambitious gull" that "lost its bearings," which simply doubles down on the joke. You could read the lost gull as Reuben describing himself, but nothing in the chat supports that, so its meaning doesn't clearly change.

**His name.** "Reuben" appears only at the end. He asks for it "when we're done," and Brick says it straight away: "Tuesday at eight, Reuben." That isn't a callback exactly, but Brick answers the request early instead of waiting.
